lines.text: There is a castle wall in your way, taller than five men, and you need to throw a rock over it.
So you lay a long beam across a frame, like a seesaw, with one arm much shorter than the other.
You put a rock on the long end and pull the short end down hard.
But one person barely moves it.
So you tie ropes to the short end, and a whole crowd yanks them at the same time.
The long arm whips up and the rock flies. This is a traction trebuchet. Crews in ancient China had up to two hundred and fifty pullers.
But no two pulls are the same, and your rocks land all over the place.
So you swap the people for a giant wooden box and fill it with stones and sand.
Hang it from the short arm on a hinge, so it falls the same way every time. This is a counterweight.
But now the long arm is far too heavy to pull down by hand.
So you add a winch, and crank until the long arm is pinned to the ground.
But the arm alone throws the rock short and low.
So you tie a rope sling to the tip. One end is fixed, the other is a loop hooked over a pin.
As the arm swings, the sling whips around, the loop slips off the pin, and the rock flies free. This is a sling.
Now you can hurl stones heavier than three grown men, or send smaller ones more than three hundred and fifty meters.
Armies kept building these until cannons took over in the fourteen hundreds.
Congratulations. You have built a trebuchet.
